clue.text: Old geographer gives nothing to London hospital in return

indicators.note: in return tells us the hospital's name is to be read from back to front

parts.note: Barts is the familiar name of St Bartholomew's Hospital in London
nothing is zero, the round letter O

explanation.surface: An ancient mapmaker makes a gift of nothing back to a London hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Barts is St Bartholomew's, London's oldest hospital; 'in return' turns only its name round. Strabo was a Greek geographer of the first century BC.
explanation.definitionFit: Strabo was a Greek scholar who wrote a vast descriptive survey of the known world.

clue.text: Fond of company. Italian and Greek islands rise to receive one

indicators.note: to receive says the islands take another letter in
in a down clue, rise means the letters are read upwards, back to front

parts.note: Elba is an Italian island, as the clue's island word implies
Cos (or Kos) is one of the Greek Dodecanese islands
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A sociable traveller notes Mediterranean islands taking in a visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: ELBA and COS take in I to make ELBAICOS; 'rise' reads that upwards in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: A gregarious person enjoys the presence of others and seeks out their companionship.

clue.text: Of independent means, is he a rip? That's right

parts.note: a rent is a rip or tear
i.e. stands for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a wealthy idler is a rascal, and is told yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is he a' only joins definition and wordplay. A 'rip' sounds like a rogue, but it is a tear.
explanation.definitionFit: A person living on income from investments or property has independent means.

clue.text: Crashing a car — habit of Toad and Co

indicators.note: crashing suggests a wreck, so these letters are smashed into a new order

explanation.surface: A tale of Mr Toad's motoring accidents, from The Wind in the Willows.
explanation.walkthrough: Toad's reckless driving in The Wind in the Willows makes 'crashing a car' a habit; the definition means frogs and toads generally.
explanation.definitionFit: This old zoological name covers the tailless amphibians, frogs and toads together.

clue.text: It's the bar of the court, there's no denying

definitions.text: It's the bar of the court, there's no denying

parts.words: It's the bar of the court, there's no denying
parts.note: reads like praise of the legal profession, but describes a legal rule that bars someone from denying what they earlier asserted

explanation.surface: Someone declares, with conviction, that the legal profession is the pride of the courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bar' is not the barristers but a legal obstacle: a court rule stopping a party from contradicting their own earlier word or conduct.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, this doctrine prevents a person from going back on a statement or act on which another relied.

clue.text: Plant benefiting from Norval's father's frugality

explanation.surface: A plant thrives on the thrift of a figure from an old play.
explanation.walkthrough: In John Home's tragedy Douglas, Norval says his father feeds his flocks on the Grampian hills, a frugal swain: a herdsman with a thrifty purse.
explanation.definitionFit: A common weed with heart-shaped seed pods; Norval's father was a thrifty flock-keeper, so his savings are a herder's wallet.

clue.text: Empty-headed, obstinate — what a reputation!

indicators.note: headed says the empty piece comes at the head, before the next word

parts.note: empty suggests nothing, the letter O
dour can mean stern and obstinate

explanation.surface: An exclamation at someone with a name for being stubborn and brainless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty-headed' looks like one adjective, but it splits: O goes at the head of DOUR. Reputation is the sense in 'in good odour'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in good or bad standing with someone is to be in good or bad odour: esteem or repute.

clue.text: Recreation when enjoyed by the older generation

definitions.text: when enjoyed by the older generation

explanation.surface: Leisure as it was enjoyed in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word as 'past time', the days the older generation enjoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobby or amusement is a recreation; the older generation's heyday was a bygone era.

clue.text: Fallen, it yells herein for mercy

indicators.note: herein says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A fallen person cries out for clemency.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenity is gentleness or leniency, the quality of showing clemency to the guilty.

clue.text: Remark about railway's first provision for sightseers

parts.note: an observation is a remark
ca, for circa, means about

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of railway's

explanation.surface: A comment on a railway's earliest arrangement for tourists.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway carriage with large windows is laid on so passengers can enjoy the scenery.

clue.text: Beat artist?

parts.note: suggests a beatnik painter, but means a police officer who walks a beat, and also a famous English landscape painter

explanation.surface: A question about a painter from the Beat Generation.
explanation.walkthrough: A police officer walks a beat; John Constable was the English painter of The Hay Wain. Both readings meet in one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A police officer on patrol shares the surname of the English Romantic landscape painter John Constable.

clue.text: Brother (or other relation) of Valentine

parts.note: taken as written
a son is another kind of family relation besides a brother

explanation.surface: A query about the family tree of someone named Valentine.
explanation.walkthrough: Valentine and Orson is a medieval romance about twin brothers separated at birth, one raised at court and one by a bear.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old French romance, the twin of the knight Valentine was raised wild in the forest.

clue.text: Stir it into stone

indicators.note: into says the word it goes inside the word for stone

parts.note: agate is a banded semi-precious stone

explanation.surface: An instruction to mix something into a stone.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir a liquid is to shake it up or set it in motion.

clue.text: Hoffmann's girl shared the fate of Belloc's Matilda

definitions.text: Hoffmann's girl shared the fate of Belloc's Matilda

parts.words: Hoffmann's girl shared the fate of Belloc's Matilda
parts.note: a literary allusion: a girl in Heinrich Hoffmann's Struwwelpeter who, like Belloc's Matilda, was burned to death

explanation.surface: A comparison between two cautionary-tale heroines who come to the same end.
explanation.walkthrough: In Struwwelpeter, the girl who plays with matches burns up; Belloc's Matilda, who told lies, also died in a fire. Hoffmann here is the author of Struwwelpeter, not E. T. A. Hoffmann.
explanation.definitionFit: The Struwwelpeter story of the matches tells of a disobedient girl who sets herself alight.

clue.text: Charles has no directions for chopping tree

indicators.note: chopping means the remaining letters are cut up and rearranged
has no says some letters are removed from the name Charles

parts.note: E and S are the compass points east and south

explanation.surface: Charles, lost without a map, sets about felling a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has no' strips E and S from CHARLES, leaving CHARL, and 'chopping' rearranges that into the tree.
explanation.definitionFit: This deciduous conifer is a common timber tree that sheds its needles in winter.

clue.text: There's nothing right in evil practices — they suck you down

indicators.note: in places the pieces before it inside the word for evil practices

parts.note: vices are immoral habits
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A moralist warns that wicked habits contain nothing good and drag you under.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition looks like part of the moral warning, but it describes whirlpools and eddies.
explanation.definitionFit: Whirlpools and eddies spin round and pull floating things downwards into their centres.

clue.text: Press annoyed by German award

parts.note: to iron is to press clothes
cross means annoyed

explanation.surface: The newspapers are angered by a decoration from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' suggests the newspapers, but it is pressing clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: This Prussian and German military decoration was awarded for bravery.

clue.text: False beard — yet was shopped

indicators.note: false means the letters are not genuine but rearranged

explanation.surface: Despite a fake beard, the fugitive was turned in to the police.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, to shop someone is to inform on them to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: To shop someone is British slang for informing on them, i.e. treacherously giving them away.

clue.text: Home for a cat-goddess but is taking in bachelors

indicators.note: taking in says the word but swallows the bachelors' letters

parts.note: BA stands for Bachelor of Arts, so bachelors are BAs

explanation.surface: Where would a feline deity live, though it puts up single men?
explanation.walkthrough: 'but is' looks like a link phrase but supplies the outer letters. The city was the cult centre of Bastet, the Egyptian cat goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: This ancient Egyptian city in the Nile delta was the main shrine of the feline deity Bastet.

clue.text: Snooty place to steal the limelight?

explanation.surface: A haughty actor positions themselves to grab attention.
explanation.walkthrough: As an adjective the word means haughty; on stage it is the rear area, from where an actor draws the audience's eyes away from others.
explanation.definitionFit: Snobbish people are standoffish; the back of the stage is where an actor can upstage colleagues facing away from the audience.

clue.text: This form of oxygen's a lightweight one

parts.note: oz, the ounce, is a small unit of weight
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chemistry note says a variety of oxygen is a featherweight.
explanation.walkthrough: OZ is the abbreviation for ounce, a very light weight.
explanation.definitionFit: This molecule of three oxygen atoms is a variant of the element, found in the upper atmosphere.

clue.text: How to get round something, or perhaps above it

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the phrase might be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Advice on dealing with an obstacle: go round it, or over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'above it' looks like the alternative to going round, but 'perhaps' makes it the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To obviate a problem is to avoid or forestall it, sidestepping a difficulty.

clue.text: Such characters are inclined to show stress

definitions.text: Such characters are inclined to show stress

parts.words: Such characters are inclined to show stress
parts.note: sounds like people who crack under pressure, but describes sloping printed letters used for emphasis

explanation.surface: A remark about the kind of people who tend to look strained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' are printed letters, 'inclined' means sloping, and 'stress' is emphasis.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloping type is used in print to emphasise words.

clue.text: Trial, say, you do of Roman military defence

parts.note: a test is a trial

indicators.note: say tells us the words you do are to be heard, not spelled out

parts.note: spoken, these two words give the sound written here as UDO

explanation.surface: A legal hearing, perhaps, conducted on the subject of ancient Rome's soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: TEST plus the sound of 'you do' gives the word. 'say' sits between the pieces but marks the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman soldiers locked their shields overhead and around them in a tortoise-like formation for protection.

clue.text: A foreign member's pacifist suggestion

parts.note: un is a in French
an arm is a limb, or member

explanation.surface: A peace activist from abroad proposes laying down weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Disarm is what a pacifist would urge; to unarm is to put away weapons.

clue.text: Reveal French article, about finished

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article
c, for circa, means about
over means finished

explanation.surface: A command to expose a French news piece that is past its time.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal something is to lay it bare or expose it to view.

clue.text: Student owns a place in Tibet

parts.note: L is the learner plate of a learner driver, so a student
has means owns
taken as written

explanation.surface: A learner possesses a property in the Himalayas.
explanation.definitionFit: This city is the capital of the Tibet region of China.

clue.text: No end of money -so cautious a bird!

indicators.note: no end of means the last letter of the word for money is dropped

parts.note: cash is money
taken as written
wary means cautious

explanation.surface: Someone with endless cash exclaims about being so careful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' cuts H from CASH, leaving CAS. 'No end of' looks like 'plenty of', but it signals the cut.
explanation.definitionFit: This large flightless Australasian bird is related to the emu.

clue.text: Cry about a mere disaster, eg milk spilt here?

indicators.note: about says the word cry goes around the other letters
disaster means the letters of a mere are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Lamenting a minor catastrophe, such as some spilt milk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' rearranges the letters to EAMER, and 'about' puts the other word round it. The proverb 'no use crying over spilt milk' colours the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A dairy is a place where milk is handled, so it is where it might get spilt.

clue.text: East German terminus for Belgian destination

parts.note: Ost is the German word for east
an end is a terminus

explanation.surface: An end-of-the-line station in East Germany serves travellers bound for Belgium.
explanation.definitionFit: This port on the Belgian coast was a common ferry arrival point from England.
